records.name: Special Region of Yogyakarta
records.current_summary:
Yogyakarta is among the eight provinces whose regional regulations OutRight's Creeping Criminalisation study examined as discriminatory, and is one of the eight (with North Sumatra) for which no specific enforcement incident, police action, or enacted anti-LGBT bylaw targeting transgender people was documented in the dossier. The signal is legal divergence without operational evidence. Despite its special administrative status and cultural prominence, no trans-specific incident was found; the OutRight finding confirms a regulatory layer but does not demonstrate enforcement against visitors.

Deviation from the national score (0.15) is −0.02, the minimum reporting threshold; Yogyakarta shares this minimal-divergence tier with North Sumatra.

It sits above the operational-enforcement provinces (Aceh 0.03, West Java 0.08, West Sumatra 0.11) where raids, corporal punishment or enacted bylaws exist, below the capital territory (0.16) - also an OutRight focus province - and below Bali (0.22), which has no documented regulatory signal and benefits from tourism-economy tolerance.

sources.claim: OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation: Mapping of Indonesia's National Laws and Regional Regulations That Violate Human Rights of Women and LGBTIQ People' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa; 2022 file copy): maps national laws and discriminatory regional regulations, examining regional regulations in eight focus provinces - Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatra, South Sulawesi, South Sumatra and Yogyakarta - finding much overlap but significant regional variation (dress codes, curfews, restrictions on where transgender people may appear), and states that its findings are valid for regions beyond the focus set.

sources.title: Pesantren Waria Yogyakarta: Kami hanya belajar agama (BBC Indonesia)
sources.claim: BBC Indonesia (26 February 2016) reports that on the night of Wednesday 24 February 2016 Yogyakarta's Pondok Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah — a religious school where trans women ('waria') study Islam — was closed after the hardline Front Jihad Islam (FJI) threatened to seal it, amid what the BBC describes as rising hate speech against LGBT people 'especially in Yogyakarta'. Banguntapan district head (camat) Jati Bayubroto justified the closure on the grounds the pesantren lacked a permit, conflicted with Islamic values and had once had alcohol found on site; founder Shinta Ratri said about 20 waria attend the weekly weekend classes, which teach ordinary Islamic instruction. The report documents a concrete, Yogyakarta-located enforcement-adjacent event against a trans institution — the first such incident this record's dossier had recorded — while showing the shutdown proceeded on administrative/religious grounds rather than an enacted regional anti-trans regulation.

sources.title: Pesantren waria di Yogyakarta ditutup sementara (Rappler Indonesia)
sources.claim: Rappler Indonesia's 25 February 2016 report details the closure meeting: on 24 February 2016 at about 20:00 WIB a two-hour meeting at the Jagalan ward office in Yogyakarta — attended by ward/residents' officials, the lurah, the local military district commander and, in the earlier 19 February session, the Banguntapan camat and the local police sector chief (Kapolsek) — ended with an agreement to shut the Al-Fatah waria pesantren after the Front Jihad Islam demanded it; a waria witness said an FJI leader delivered 'fiery' anti-LGBT remarks to shouts of 'Allahu Akbar' and vowed the group would keep hunting LGBTI people wherever they gather. The Governor of the Special Region of Yogyakarta, Sultan Hamengku Buwono X, publicly urged restraint on both sides, calling LGBT people 'sama-sama anak bangsa' (fellow children of the nation) and saying the regional government would study the issue. It is the first documented Yogyakarta operational-pressure event for this record's dossier, concluded on administrative/community grounds without any provincial anti-trans statute being cited.

sources.title: Wajah Solidaritas Waria Yogyakarta di Tengah Pandemi (DW Indonesia)
sources.claim: DW Indonesia (21 June 2021) reports that Yogyakarta's trans women ('transpuan'/'waria') — most working as street performers or wedding make-up artists and attached to the Pesantren Waria Al-Fatah — saw earnings fall by about 60 percent during the COVID-19 pandemic and were, in DW's words, 'ignored by the government', struggling to pay rent and buy food. The article describes a 12 June 2021 aromatherapy-candle making class at the Al-Fatah pesantren in Yogyakarta run with local small business Malini.yk to teach new income skills, and says the waria kept performing despite donors refusing even masked performances. It shows the Yogyakarta waria community and pesantren operating again years after the 2016 closure, while documenting persistent economic and social marginalisation of trans people in the province.

records.name: Nothern Cape
records.current_summary:
The single documented trans-specific violent incident in this dossier occurred here: on 14 May 2024 in Upington, 27-year-old transgender woman Jo-Ann Isaks was stabbed multiple times and her body set on fire in her own room, discovered by a family member who noticed the house burning. TGEU's Trans Day of Remembrance register records the killing and notes that "the LGBTIQ+ community in the Northern Cape has been shaken" - a province-level community response in a small province where one violent death is a meaningful rate observation. Police opened a murder case and reported no arrests at the time of the entry; the register records that police 'identified' the decedent by a deadname.

The killing is a lone incident and not clearly patterned or state-implicated; there is no evidence of impunity or victim-prosecution in the dossier, and no provincial legislative or enforcement finding against trans visitors. The score therefore reflects severity-dominant weighting: the method (burning) is extreme and the community-level shock signal is real, but the single-incident rule cautions against large score moves from an unpatterned crime. Northern Cape does not appear in the customary-authority / traditional-court geography and has no identified institutional climate finding.

The score is 0.05 below the national 0.69. vs. Gauteng (0.71) and Western Cape (0.72), the gap is driven by a concrete trans-identified murder and the small-population rate effect rather than by any jurisdictional or legislative divergence. vs. Mpumalanga (0.65) and Limpopo (0.65), the Northern Cape sits at a similar level: Mpumalanga/Limpopo carry diffuse institutional-climate and jurisdictional risk without a single trans-specific incident, whereas Northern Cape has one severe incident without patterned institutional backing. The dossier's under-reporting caveat means other provinces may experience similar violence without it reaching TGEU's register.

sources.claim: TGEU Trans Day of Remembrance register entry (14 May 2024): Jo-Ann Isaks, 27, a transgender woman, was found dead in a burning room in the Paballelo location of Upington after multiple stab wounds; a family member noticed the fire at about 23:00. Police (ZF Mgcawu District) confirmed a murder case, with no arrests at the time of the entry, and referred to the decedent by a deadname; the entry quotes district LGBTIQ+ leader Jenny Sambok and reports the province's LGBTIQ+ community 'shaken'.

sources.title: Upington Transgender Woman Murdered in Suspected Hate Crime (MambaOnline)
sources.claim: MambaOnline (24 May 2024) reports that on the night of Wednesday 14 May 2024, 27-year-old transgender woman Jo-Ann Isaks was found dead in her burning room in Paballelo township, Upington, after a family member saw flames at about 23:00 and discovered her body — already alight — with multiple stab wounds to the upper body. ZF Mgcawu District Municipality police spokesperson Sgt Omphile Masegela confirmed a murder case had been opened, called the investigation 'at a critical stage', reported no arrests at that date, and police publicly identified the victim as 'Jonathan Isaks' — the deadnaming this record's TGEU entry also recorded. Northern Cape LGBTIQ+ district leader Jenny Sambok said the community in the ZF Mgcawu region had been shaken, providing the local community-level response this dossier cites.

sources.title: Transgender Kimberley High School Teen Murdered in Suspected Hate Crime (MambaOnline)
sources.claim: MambaOnline (13 June 2024) reports that on 1 June 2024, 18-year-old transgender learner Karabelo Pudumo — a Grade 10 student at Pescodia High School who lived with her grandparents — was stabbed to death in Kimberley, capital of the Northern Cape; a man she had been drinking with allegedly turned on her after realising she was transgender, stabbing her more than 20 times. A suspect was reportedly arrested, though MambaOnline could not verify this with authorities, and more than 300 children and community members attended a memorial service at the school. The killing is the second suspected hate-crime murder of a transgender person in the Northern Cape within a month — after Jo-Ann Isaks' 14 May death in Upington — giving this record's dossier patterning evidence beyond a single incident.

sources.title: Kimberley to Host First-Ever Northern Cape Pride (MambaOnline)
sources.claim: MambaOnline (2 November 2024) reports the inaugural Northern Cape Pride, set for 30 November 2024 at Kimberley's Galeshewe Open Air Arena under the theme 'Pride with a Purpose', featuring a morning parade, speakers and community activities, with Pride Committee member Tebogo Makwati calling it a historic moment for the province. The article also records that the province saw at least three LGBTIQ+ community members murdered in 2024: Jo-Ann Isaks (27, transgender woman, May), Karabelo Pudumo (18, transgender high school student, June) and a 50-year-old gay man, Lazarus Ikaneng Thomas (September). It documents both organised community presence and the year's third and latest killing of an LGBTIQ+ person in the Northern Cape.

records.name: Limpopo
records.current_summary:
Limpopo's rural life runs through chiefs and traditional courts to a degree that makes the parallel customary-law system the province's defining risk factor. Human Rights Watch's analysis of the legislation at issue warned that it 'establishes a separate legal system for people living in the former Bantustans' and 'threatens to undermine this security for millions of South Africans living in rural areas', 'particularly for the exercise of gender and sexual rights' — because chiefs and traditional courts adjudicate personal-status and morality-adjacent matters under customary law, with a consent presumption running against the individual. The later record, from a 2025 verification pass: the bill was enacted as the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act of 2019, and was then declared unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court in 2023, with the declaration suspended and the Act's validity extended while Parliament works on a replacement. A 2012 activist report — 'culture of the chiefs threatens our rights' — pressed the same case contemporaneously.

No statute criminalises a visitor's expression here and no trans-specific incident series is recorded. But for an outed visitor in rural Limpopo, the practical moral authority is often the chief's court rather than the ordinary court — and that jurisdiction's record on gender and sexuality runs against the individual. The absence of recorded incidents reflects under-reporting, not demonstrated safety.
records.current_outOfScope: The absence of retrievable incidents here reflects an under-reporting problem in the sources, not confirmed safety; the province's finding is jurisdictional (density of functioning traditional authority).

sources.claim: HRW (29 May 2012): the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament threatened LGBT South Africans by creating a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustans; HRW reports rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas, and the bill offered no opt-out from customary jurisdiction. Supports the province's framing of traditional-court rural jurisdiction as the defining risk factor for LGBT travellers off the main cities.

Mamba Online (18 Apr 2012, Melanie Judge): the Traditional Courts Bill debated in provincial public hearings would re-criminalise gay and lesbian conduct in former-Bantustan areas through a separate customary system; lesbians are reported punished at chiefs' homesteads and tribal offices with no opt-out, so those who can are expected to leave rural areas; traditional leaders also opposed the 2006 Civil Union Act. Direct support for the record's rural-traditional-courts risk assessment.

freshness_all.fact: Chiefs/customary-court authority issue remains live: Constitutional Court (CCT73/22, 2023) invalidated parts of the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act but suspended the declaration pending fix; 2012-era sources remain directionally current, not superseded.

The 2012-bill threat HRW described was later enacted (2019) and then invalidated in Mogale (2023), so the source's framing is two legal generations behind.

records.name: Eastern Cape
records.current_summary:
The Eastern Cape is listed among the former-Bantustan provinces where traditional-court jurisdiction operates—HRW's analysis of the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act identifies the rural gender/sexual-rights exposure under customary adjudication—but no trans-specific incident, statute, enforcement action, or institutional statement was found for this province. The dossier states plainly: "Free State and Eastern Cape have no trans-specific source at all." Provincial violence against women and girls is severe (multiple 2025 mass-casualty killings in Gqeberha), but arrests followed each incident (four suspects for the May 2025 killings, four for the June 2025 burning of teenagers at KwaNobuhle, charges against a police officer for the July 2025 killings at Gordon Terrace), and none of the victims is identified as trans. The arrests represent a functioning—if strained—state-response mechanism, which is a small positive against the backdrop of extreme national violent-crime rates.

For a visitor, the practical exposure is the general South African violent-crime baseline (national, priced into the 0.69) plus the township-and-rural customary-authority axis where a visibly gender-nonconforming person outside the metro NGO belt is more likely to encounter a chief's moral adjudication than a magistrate's court. No province-level ban, no enforcement against expression, no religious criminal law. The Constitutional Court's Mogale invalidity of the TKLA and the suspended replacement reduce but do not eliminate the parallel-system concern.

The score is 0.02 below the national 0.69. vs. Limpopo (0.65) and North West (0.65), the Eastern Cape sits higher because its traditional-authority density is lower (the dossier groups Limpopo/North West as the provinces where "traditional-court jurisdiction actually bites" most strongly), and the 2025 arrests demonstrate at least nominally functioning state enforcement in the metro (Gqeberha). vs. Gauteng (0.71) and Western Cape (0.72), the gap reflects the absence of a metro NGO/prosecutor belt and the rural customary-authority geography. vs. KwaZulu-Natal (0.63), the Eastern Cape's lower deviation from national reflects the absence of a retrieved trans-specific study or royal/CONTRALESA episode in this province.
records.current_outOfScope: The province's 2025 mass-casualty killings of women and girls are gender-based violence against females, none of the victims identified as trans; they are recorded as severe general-crime context, not as trans findings.

sources.claim: HRW (29 May 2012): the Traditional Courts Bill then before parliament threatened LGBT South Africans by creating a parallel customary-law justice system covering people in the former Bantustans; HRW reports rural LGBT people already face discrimination, violence and poor police cooperation, chiefs' courts punish lesbians in rural areas, and the bill offered no opt-out from customary jurisdiction. Supports the province's framing of traditional-court rural jurisdiction as the defining risk factor for LGBT travellers off the main cities.

1st Afrika (2 May 2025): Eastern Cape police arrested four suspects over the killings of two women in Gqeberha whose bodies were found at separate locations the prior week; the murders sparked public outrage and renewed calls to confront rising gender-based violence in the province. Regional violent-incident context for traveller safety.

records.name: Western Cape
records.current_summary:
The Western Cape is the one province the dossier identifies as "usually scored as safest," with the strongest NGO infrastructure and the highest public visibility (Cape Town). No province-specific trans threat, ban, statute, enforcement action, or violent incident was found. For a foreign visitor, the practical implication is that the institutional response to a discovered trans person is a metro court, a PEPUDA-trained magistrate, and a visible civil-society network—the tier of protection that South Africa's constitutional enumeration of gender identity actually reaches in practice. The Hate Crime framework and the constitutional equality clause operate through functioning, accessible metro institutions here more than anywhere else in the country.

One unresolved sub-national question: Khoi-San communities in the Western Cape are pressing for recognition of indigenous authority structures unrecognised for three decades while Nguni chiefs are, with litigation over intangible cultural heritage (Khoin v Jenkins, 2022/2023). This is a parallel-authority recognition question in the safest province, not an existing jurisdiction that adjudicates gender or morality—no chief's court currently operates against a visitor in the Western Cape, and the litigation concerns cultural-heritage recognition, not criminal or moral adjudication of queer people. It is a small uncertainty against an otherwise clean provincial record.

The score is 0.03 above the national 0.69. vs. Gauteng (0.71), the Western Cape sits marginally higher because it has the highest public visibility and the strongest NGO infrastructure per capita, with a lower recorded-violence volume; both are metro-institution provinces but the Cape's NGO belt is more concentrated and accessible. vs. Limpopo (0.65) and North West (0.65), the gap of 0.07 reflects a fully functioning state-institution environment with active civil society against a rural customary-authority geography where the state's moral adjudication is mediated by a chief's court. vs. KwaZulu-Natal (0.63), the gap of 0.09 reflects the absence of a documented township queerphobia study and the absence of any royal or chiefly authority publicly aligning against queer people. vs. Northern Cape (0.64), the gap reflects a functioning institutional environment against a province that has produced a recorded trans murder.
records.current_outOfScope: Cape Town's visibility and NGO infrastructure are province-level strengths, but violent-crime exposure in the province is part of South Africa's national general-crime baseline and not trans-specific.

sources.claim: FF+-carried opinion piece (17 October 2025): Khoi and San communities remain officially unrecognised after three decades while Nguni groups benefit under existing legislation; notes the Constitutional Court's 14 October 2025 ruling suspending the declaration of invalidity of the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act for two years, to 29 May 2027, pending a replacement.

Peter Kantor, case note (2023, PER/PELJ vol. 26) on 'Khoin v Jenkins in re: Observatory Civic Association v Trustees ... Liesbeek Leisure Properties Trust' [2023] 1 All SA 110 (WCC): analyses the Western Cape High Court appeal decision on intangible cultural heritage and failure to consult First Nations communities - judicial recognition of 'intangible heritage' in South African heritage law; a cultural-heritage recognition dispute, not a morality or criminal jurisdiction.

sources.title: Trans Woman Stands Her Ground After Stadium Bathroom Incident in Cape Town
sources.claim: Taswald Ruiters, a transgender woman from Eerste River, Cape Town, was threatened with removal from the Green Point Athletic Stadium on 19 February 2025 after using the women's bathroom; a security guard told her 'Look at you, you're a man', ordered her to use the men's bathroom and claimed he had the final say, and police called four times never arrived in nearly three hours, MambaOnline reported on 28 February 2025. The stadium is a public facility operated by the City of Cape Town, with the venue rented on the day by Western Province Athletics, which was responsible for the security services. Records the enforcement-and-response gap a visibly trans visitor can meet in the province's best-resourced metro, without any provincial rule restricting bathroom use by trans people.

records.name: Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur
records.current_summary:
PACA deviates −0.02 from the national 0.67. The region-specific negative is the RN mayor of Fréjus, David Rachline, issuing an arrêté on 1 August 2023 prohibiting swimming on communal beaches for anyone wearing "covering and loose clothing"—a dress-code order whose language directly reaches gender-nonconforming public appearance. However, the Toulon administrative tribunal suspended the arrêté and condemned the commune to €3,000 in August 2023, a clear institutional pushback. Per the enforcement-over-statute rule, a court-blocked municipal order carries small weight; its residual harm is the chilling signal it sends to a visitor who sees public dress policed by mayoral fiat, even if the specific order no longer operates.

PACA also shares Marseille's metro exposure: urban units over 200,000 record 9 per 100,000 anti-LGBT offences against the national average of 7, a pattern driven by reporting density and visibility as much as by elevated actual incidence. The region's net position mirrors Île-de-France (0.65): a small negative from a specific municipal incident partially offset by a strong judicial correction, set against an urban-rate backdrop that the dossier explicitly cautions against reading as danger.

Compare with Hauts-de-France (0.64), where the RN pattern spans multiple communes and "around thirty associations" without a comparable single court suspension to offset it; PACA's one documented arrêté was fully and quickly reversed. Compare with Bourgogne-Franche-Comté (0.62), where the prefecture's ban was upheld rather than overturned—a materially different judicial outcome that justifies the spread between 0.62 and 0.65.
records.current_outOfScope: General urban crime in Marseille and tourist-season congestion affect all travellers; the region-level concern for trans visitors is municipal dress-policing precedent, not street crime.

sources.claim: France 3 Régions (Var): Fréjus's RN mayor issued an order of 1 Aug 2023 banning 'covering and baggy clothing' while swimming in sea beaches, running to 17 Sep 2023 with a €135 fine; the administrative court of Toulon suspended it on 5 Aug 2023 and ordered the town to pay €3,000. The article quotes observers noting the mayor justified the ban on laïcité in the communiqué while citing safety publicly — framing religiously-marked swimwear as the target. Context: a similar Mandelieu-la-Napoule burkini ban had already been rejected (with Ligue des droits de l'homme contesting). Relevant here as gendered/religious beachwear policing of visible non-conformity on this region's beaches — now legally blocked.

Full text of the Toulon administrative tribunal's freedom-of-relief order n° 2302537 of 5 August 2023 (LDH v Fréjus commune): suspends execution of the 1 August 2023 beach dress-code arrêté as a grave and manifestly unlawful attack on fundamental freedoms (manifestation of religious conviction, freedom of movement, freedom of dress in public space), following the Conseil d'État's 17 July 2023 ruling on the identical Mandelieu-la-Napoule arrêté; the commune is condemned to pay the LDH €3,000.

freshness_all.fact: Judgment text paywalled (lexisnexis) and news search for TA Toulon 2023 no.2302537 returned nothing; subject and current appeal status undetermined.

records.name: Kabardino-Balkaria
records.current_summary:
The UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025) places the North Caucasus — this republic among them — in the category where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, and documents systematic campaigns against LGBT+ people across the region from 2017 to 2024 including abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings. North Caucasus SOS's judgement that there is “no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus”, with private existence able to trigger violence, detention or forced return to families, encompasses the republic, and the organisation says the situation worsens year on year.

No Chechnya-scale extrajudicial detention or purge infrastructure is documented here, and the republic carries no special-permission entry requirement of the kind Western advisories attach to some other North-Caucasus republics (it is flagged in Canadian guidance only for general security near the Georgian border). The applicable risk is the regional one: the 2023 federal ‘extremist’ designation operating through security structures and family-honour norms that can produce violence and informal detention outside legal process.
records.current_outOfScope: The republic's general risks - elevated tensions toward the Georgian border and mountaineering-area advisories cited for all travellers - sit outside trans-specific risk.

sources.claim: Human Rights House Foundation interview with David Isteev (North Caucasus SOS): 'There is no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus, and even private existence can trigger violence, detention, or forced return to families'; annual deterioration attested by an on-the-ground defender working in exile. Regional testimony underpinning this record's risk framing.

UK Home Office country policy note, Russia, SOGI (June 2025): treats the North Caucasus (incl. this republic) as the exception to its otherwise non-persecutory Russia finding — trans people and public LGBT+ advocates in the region likely to face treatment amounting to persecution; documents systematic regional campaigns 2017–2024; 2023 'extremist' designation exposes LGBT+ activity to 2–6 (organising 6–10) years' imprisonment, violence spreading beyond the region.

records.name: NCR
records.current_summary:
The Philippines has no national anti-discrimination statute covering gender identity; the national picture is violence against trans women, documented in a 2024–2025 series of killings, without dependable local machinery. The capital region carries the country's strongest local protections: in July 2025 Quezon City became its first local government unit to enact a Gender-Inclusive Health Ordinance, creating a framework for gender-affirming primary care, mental-health support and specialist services through the city's public-health system — the only enforceable institutional recourse a discovered visitor can find anywhere in the archipelago.

Lethal violence is on the regional record too: the transrespectful memorial lists Shaina Bayabay, 29, strangled during a drinking session in Pasig City, Metro Manila, on 1 March 2024. Protection here is real but partial — a functioning framework on paper in the country's largest city, and an enforcement-and-services reality that does not yet extend past city limits.
records.current_localsOnly: The Gender-Inclusive Health Ordinance's clinical services - gender-affirming primary care and mental-health support in city facilities - are what residents use; what a visitor can actually invoke is the anti-discrimination complaint machinery (the QC Gender Desk and city health office routes).

sources.claim: Quezon City government: ordinance by Councilors Bernard Herrera et al. makes all city public health facilities offer gender-affirming consultations and counselling, mental health support, and medical guidance/referrals regardless of gender identity or expression; Mayor Joy Belmonte says it removes longstanding healthcare barriers for gender-diverse and transgender residents - concrete municipal-level protection inside Metro Manila.

Transrespectful/trans murder documentation site (TDoR2 memorial) report entry: Shaina Bayabay, 29, Pasig City, Metro Manila, Philippines - 1 March 2024, category violence, cause strangled; the underlying report adds that she was killed during a drinking session.
